3019: The petitioner, a member of the Indian Army, was dismissed from service by an order dated March 31, 1962. The Central Government rejected the petition on the ground that r. 14 of the Army Rules, 1954, which were framed in exercise of the powers conferred by section 191 of the , had been ultra vires the Act. The High Court held that r.14 was intra vires and quashed the order of dismissal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that (i) the Central Government could not have passed the impugned order; (ii) the Central Gove rnment had no power to make rules providing for removal from service of persons subject to the Act; (iii) the Central Govt. had no jurisdiction to pass the impugned order. HELD: (1) The Central Government has no power to remove a person from service under section 19 of the read with r. 14. The Central Govt. is empowered to remove a member of a court martial if he is found guilty of any offence or misconduct specified in the Act. [880 B] (2) The Central Govt., having power to remove an officer from service under the proviso to sub section (3) of section 19 of Act, is also competent to remove him from service. The Central Govemment can do so only after following the procedure prescribed by law. [881 C D] (3) The Central Goverr ment cannot be compelled to follow the provisions of the Act. It is open to the Central Gover nment to remove a particular officer from service without complying with the requirements of the Act and the rules made thereunder. But the Central Gov ernment cannot act arbitrarily or mala fide. [882 E F]

2124: The appellant was a resident of the State of West Bengal. He filed an election petition challenging his election to the West Bengal Legislative Assembly on the ground that he belonged to a Scheduled Caste in West Bengal and that he had been wrongly excluded from the Schedule of the West Bengal Legislature. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appellant was not a member of the Scheduled Castes specified in item 40 of Part I of the Schedule to the Order which set out the Scheduled Castes in West Bengal as one of the castes mentioned in item 40, and that the appellant did not belong to the Schedule caste specified in item40. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the appellant was a Sunri by caste but was excluded from the Scheduled Caste group because he belonged to the Saha caste group; (ii) the appellant had no connection with the Sahas formed for a long time past; (iii) the appellant could not be said to belong to the Saha community which was a scheduled caste within the meaning of section 2(1)(d) of the West Bihar Act, 1950, and (iv) the appellant 's case was not covered by any of the exceptions to section 123 of the Act. HELD: (i) The appellant was not entitled to challenge the validity of the order of the High Court rejecting his election petition. [380 D] (ii) The appellant had not been able to establish that he belonged either to a Scheduled caste or to a Schedule caste specified under item 40 of the Order. [381 G] (iii) The appellant did not claim to belong to a Scheduled Tribe in West Bengal. His claim was therefore rightly rejected. [382 E]
78: The appellant was charged under section 18(1) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 for receiving a sum or consideration as a condition for the reli gishment of his tenancy. He was convicted under section 19(2) of the Act and sentenced to one day 's simple imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 30,000. The High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to one day's simple imprisonment. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (a) the word "relinquish ment" in section 18(I) of the said Act meant only an act of relinquishment and not a mere creation of a right; (b) the word 'relinquishment ' is used in the section with reference to the circumstances of the case and in its widest sense; (c) the word has been used in the context of the provisions of the Act which are intended to be applied to cases where the tenant had no right to the premises and had no right of occupation thereof; (d) the word is used in a comprehensive sense and in its popular sense, meaning "the act of relinquishing possession of the tenant by the landlord". HELD : (1) The word "relating" in section 2(g) of the Rent Act means the same thing as referring to something done or to be done or taken in law or in fact in force in the premises. [423 D] (2)The word "related" in section 19(1) refers to any person who was in occupation of the premises on the date of the commencement of the Act. It does not refer to any person claiming or receiving any rent from him. [422 F H] (3)The word 'related' in section 18 (I) of Act means the person who actually occupies the premises on behalf of the tenant. [424 A B] (4)Section 18(I)(e) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, provides that if the tenant makes default in payment of rent he shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months. [425 C]
4316: The appellant company was a partnership firm. Its work force consists of engineers and supervisors and different categories of workmen. They served a Charter of Demands in July, 1974 on the appellant and as their demands were not accepted and conciliation proceedings proved fruitless. The appellant filed a statement before the Tribunal claiming an upward revision of the wage scales and dearness allowance and an increase from fifteen years to twenty years in the span for earning annual increments. The Union also filed a statement stating that the existing wage scales were fair and reasonable on a region cum industry basis and that it would not be possible for the appellant to bear the additional financial burden if the demands of the union were accepted. The Tribunal rejected the claim of the Union and held that the existing wages had been properly revised by the appellant. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The Tribunal has rightly given a flat increase of Rs. 150/ in the category of Draughtsmen and Rs. 100/ in the case of other categories. [174E] (2) The Tribunal found that the existing pay scale was fair and reasonable. It is true that besides the staff of 306 workmen represented by the Union there were several other employees who would also have to be paid, the Tribunal considered it fair in paragraph 23 of the award. But the Tribunal did not take into account the fact that the existing workers represented by the union were also equally qualified. [175B C] (3) The Tribunal was right in holding that the existing rates of wages should be revised. [176D] (4) The Tribunal had correctly taken into consideration the fact that there was no material to show that the existing grades were either less or more than those of the existing grades. [177A] (5) The Tribunal could not have gone behind the figures of the existing wage structure and the number of years which elapsed since the award was made. [178C]
314: The appellant was put up for trial before the Sessions Judge, Patiala. He pleaded guilty to the charge under section 465 of the Indian Penal Code and was convicted by the Sessions Judge under section 409 of the Indian penal Code. The High Court set aside his conviction on the ground that sanction under section 197(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure had not been obtained. Held, that the prosecution which has resulted in the conviction of the appellant was initiated without any sanction under section 19 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, and if it is held that the prosecution was instituted without any sanction, the material on record did not justify a reversal of that verdict by the appellate court. The order of acquittal passed by the Sessions judge was not vitiated by reason of any error of law or procedure having been committed by him. The order was legal and valid. The appeal must therefore be allowed. The appellant was entitled to an acquittal. The order setting aside the order of acquittal was illegal because the sanction under section 13 of the Prevention Of Corruption Act was necessary when the act complained of was done while the accused was actually engaged in the performance of official duties.

2796: The appellants were convicted under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to 5 years rigorous imprisonment. They were also convicted under section 412 of the Indian penal Code and sentenced by the trial court to 5 years Rigorous Imprisonment. The High Court acquitted them on the ground that the prosecution had failed to prove the case against them beyond reasonable doubt. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The presumption that they were dacoits ought not to have been drawn since the circumstances do not admit the drawing of such a presumption in the case. [154 D] (2) The presumption which arises from the fact that the stolen property was recovered from the possession of one person does not mean that the presumption is rebutted by other evidence. It only means that the person who has committed the offence can be presumed to be involved in it. If he fails to establish his identity, the presumption will operate as a bar to the conviction of the accused. [155 E F] (3) There is no other evidence in the case which points out the complicity of the appellants in the crime itself. The High court did not draw any adverse inference against the appellants for want of proof of their identity. [156 A B] (4) The presumption under section 114 of the Evidence Act must be raised in the case if the facts are proved beyond all reasonable doubts. [157 C] (5) The presumptions under section 114 are rebuttable. The burden of proving the existence of circumstances bringing the case within any of the exceptions is on the accused. But the standard of proof required in the latter class of cases is not the same as in the case of proof of guilt by direct or circumstantial evidence but on the basis of preponderance of probabilities. [158 H; 159 A B]

The definition of "business" in section 2 (12) of Income tax Act is wide enough to include all activities relating to the business of the assessee. [809E F] 1.3. The expression 'profits and gains '

5266: The appellants were the owners of a piece of land in Calcutta. They leased out the land to the respondent for a period of 20 years. The lease was extended from time to time and the lease expired on September 30, 1960. The respondent filed an application under section 8(1)(a) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, before the District Judge praying that the land be declared as surplus. The appellants contended that the land had been acquired by the Government for the purpose of the company and that the company was not entitled to any compensation. The District Judge held that the land was not needed for the company 's purpose and dismissed the application. On appeal, the High Court held that the company could not be said to have been in need of money for the purpose it was intended to acquire. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The decision taken by the Government of West Bengal was neither unreasonable nor arbitrary. [844 C] (ii) The Government of West Ben gal had no power to take away the land without following the procedure prescribed by law. [845 D] (iii) The Government had no power under section 8 (1) (a) of Act, 1894 to take possession of the land which was in its possession. [846 A] (iv) The Government has no power to give directions under section 8 of the Act. [847 B] (v) The Government cannot take over the land without complying with the provisions of the Act and the Rules made thereunder. [848 E]
5248: The assessee was a Hindu Undivided Family. He had maintained an account in the books of his father, and on 1st January, 1957, he wrote to the Company stating that he had decided to gift away for love and affection various sums to the following persons: (1) Pravin, (2) Tika Ram & Sons, (3) Pravinsinh, (4) Tikarams, (5) Tukarams, and (6) Tulsidas. It was also stated that the donee had informed him that he would not make any gift out of the amount received by him. On the same day, the assessee had addressed a letter to the Company asking for crediting his account to the extent of Rs.67,560/12/ and credit the respective amounts in the names of the aforesaid persons. The assessee could not have been allowed to take advantage of the provisions of section 64(i)(a) of the Act because the transaction was not a transfer of property in goods for cash or deferred payment. [125 D] (2) The assessee had not given any explanation as to how the money was transferred to his wife. The assessee has failed to prove that the money was in fact transferred to his son. The
2304: The appellant was appointed as a District Judge in the Orissa Superior Judicial Service. He was transferred to the Orissa Super Judiciary on October 10, 1966. In September 1966, he was posted as a district judge at the time of his initial appointment. On November 16, 1966, the High Court issued an order transferring him from one post to another. The appellant challenged the order by way of a writ petition before the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the power to transfer a district judge from one post or the cadre of district judges to another is not vested with the Governor; (ii) the High Court had no authority to pass an order transferring a district judge to another post and (iii) the High court could not be said to have acted without jurisdiction in transferring the appellant from one post/village to another. HELD: (1) The High Court has no power to issue an order of transfer of a district judge. [817 B] (2) The High Courts are competent to make rules for the convenient transaction of business of the High Court. These rules are framed under article 309 of the Constitution. They are made under article 234. The High Court is competent to make such rules. [818 C D] (3) The High court can exercise its powers under article 235 only when there is a clear violation of the control vested in it by article 23. Article 235 does not confer any power upon the High Court to make rules regulating the conditions of service of persons holding posts in the judicial service of the State. [819 E F] (4) The High 'Court is not invested with the power to make rules under article 309 merely because the Government makes rules in that behalf. [820 G H]
6881: The appellant was the owner of agricultural land and village immovable property. He sold it to a purchaser who held a share in the property. The vendor sold it to the appellant who was the purchaser of the share of the vendor. The vendor filed a suit for pre emption claiming that he had purchased the share of his vendor from the appellant. The suit was dismissed by the trial court but on appeal, the High Court allowed the appeal holding that the vendor was entitled to pre emption under section 15(1)(a) of the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The right of pre emption conferred on the kinsfolk is not an absolute right which can be exercised only if there are two conditions precedent to the exercise of the right namely, (a) that the person claiming pre emption must have been a member of the joint Hindu family; and (b) that he should have been a co sharer in the joint family property. [124A B] (ii) The right to pre emotion is not an essential part of the right to preemect a member of a joint Hindu family. It is a mere statutory right. It is not a right to preemption. It is merely a statutory right. The right of the pre emption is not an enduring right. It has to be exercised with the object of protecting the members of the family or the members of their families against injury caused by the operation of the law. [125B C] Baijnath Singh vs State of Bihar, ; , followed.
6668: The appellant, who was the father of the respondents 1 to 3 and the second respondent, filed a suit for declaration that he had not been paid Rs.1 lakh as stipulated in the compromise deed executed by the father and his two sons and that he had no intention to accept the compromise. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the sale deeds were valid and the alienations were valid and that the alienees had become owners of the property. The first appellate court confirmed the decree passed by the trial court. In second appeal, the High Court held that the alienations are valid and the transferees have become owners of their property. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1.1 The alienation is valid and the transfers effected on 21st August 1987 are valid and binding. [766C] 1.2 The alienee respondent No. 2 has accepted the fact that the parties have signed the compromise petition which contains terms which they had accepted and all parties have accepted the document of compromise to be genuine. The alienees have now been brought on record as the purchasers. The alienors shall deliver vacant possession of the property by 30th April, 1991, to Seshiah and in the event of failure to do so the Trial Court is directed by this Court to deliver vacant possession. [767E F] 1.3 The alienees shall deliver vacant land to the alienees on or before 31st of April, 1991. If the alienees fail to do so, the trial court will proceed with the matter in accordance with law. [768F G] 1.4 The alienees would be entitled to retain the possession of the entire property in suit including those which are subject matter of dispute to third parties. If the alienation is not made within the time prescribed, the alienees will be entitled to take back the possession of such property from the alienees. 415: The appellant was detained under the Bombay Prohibition Act, 1949. He challenged his detention by a writ petition in the High Court of Bombay on the ground that he had been deprived of his right to make an effective representation against his detention and that the order of detention was mala fide. The High Court dismissed the petition but granted a certificate under article 133(1)(c) of the Constitution. Held: (i) The order of detention made by the State Government was not in accordance with law and was therefore illegal. It was not necessary for the detaining authority to communicate the grounds of detention to the detenu as it is implicit in section 7 of the Act that the grounds must be communicated to him. (ii)The order of detention could not be said to have been made mala fide because the detaining authority did not apply its mind to the question whether the grounds were sufficient or not. (iii)The order was bad because the detaining authorities did not inform the detenu that they would furnish the grounds of his detention. (iv)The order could not be held to be mala fide merely because the detaining officer did not inform him that the grounds of the detention were available to the detenu.
2248: The appellant was a Panchayat and its members were the Sarpanch of the respondent Panchayat. The appellant, a Panchayat, passed resolution No. 2 with a view to levy octroi duty on the goods coming within its local limits as per the Schedule 1 of the Rules. The resolution was passed by the Panchayat and it was published in the Gazette. On July 14, 1961, the Panchayat passed resolution No, 2 fixing octroi limits and number of octroi posts and place etc. It was also mentioned that the appellant would be levying octroi duty at the rate of Rs. 5/- per tonne. The appellant filed an appeal under section 124(5) of the Bombay Village Panchayats Act, 1958 before the Panchayat Samiti, Parseoni. The Panchayat Samiti allowed the appeal of the appellant and imposed octroi duty on goods coming within the local limits as prescribed by r. 21 of the Rules, calling for objections for the tax and taking of decisions thereon after the consideration, number of octroi post and place etc., should be got decided by the appropriate authority. The appellant thereupon preferred a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the resolution No. 3. The High Court held that the resolution No, 4 was not valid because it had failed to fix the octroi limits in accordance with law. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: (1) The resolution No. 5 was not invalid because it did not specify the limits of octroi posts or places. The resolution did not specify any particular octroi post or place. The resolution merely stated that the appellant was importing tea within the limits of the Panchayat. The resolution does not say that the appellant had imported tea outside the limits of Panchayat. [817 E] (2) The resolution was not bad because it did no specify the limits. The resolution could only be challenged if it was ultra vires. [818 B] (3) The resolution did no mention the limits of taxes. The resolution is therefore bad because it has not specified the limits of taxation. [819 C] (4) The resolution does no mention the limit of taxes. It is not necessary that the tax must be levied in accordance with the law. [820 D]
5142: The petitioner was detained under section 3(2) of the , on the ground that he was a dangerous person. The order of detention stated that the petitioner 's activities were prejudicial to maintenance of public order. The order also stated that the detenu was arrested in connection with the case and was produced before the Magistrate. The petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging his detention on the grounds: (i) that the detaining authority had not applied its mind to the question whether it was necessary to detain him; (ii) that the order of detention was passed mechanically without application of mind; (iii) that the detenu had been denied an opportunity to make a representation against his detention; and (iv) that the detention order was mala fide. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the order could only be justified against a person in detention if the detaining authority was satisfied that his release from detention was imminent and the order of preventive detention was necessary for putting him back in jail. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 It is well settled that the power of preventive detention is a precautionary power exercised in reasonable anticipation and has a sufficient extent. It must be exercised with a view to prevent apprehended objectionable activities. [910B] 1.2 In the instant case, the detaining authority did not apply its mind to this aspect of the matter. The order clearly shows that the detaining authorit y was satisfied that the detenu 's activities would be prejudicial to the maintenance of public Order. [911C D] 1.3 There can be no doubt that the detaining autho rity was aware of the fact that the detenu is already in custody. The detaining authority was fully aware of the facts mentioned in the order of the detaining authority. [912E F] 1.4 The detaining authority had considered all the relevant aspects including the fact that there was likelihood of the detenu being released on bail. The detaining authoritY had given a detailed reason for rejecting the request for bail. The order does not indicate any such consideration. [913F] 1.5 The detaining authority has not indicated as to what was the compelling reasons for the detaining authority to pass the order
2065: The appellants, who were the trustees of a temple in the State of Madras, filed a suit against respondents Nos. 1 to 3 and 4, who claimed title to the properties in suit on the ground that they had been granted in Inam to the ancestor of one Ambalathadum Pachai Kandai Udayavar by the former Archakas of the said temple. The case was that the said properties belonged to the temple and were alienated from time to time, and as a result of the last alienation, the appellants became entitled to them. The trial court held that the appellants had proved their title to the property in suit and that the respondents had failed to prove that the original grant had been made by the manager of the temple. On appeal, the District Judge held that the respondents could not be allowed to take advantage of the provisions of section 87 of the Act, and dismissed the suit. In second appeal, the High Court held that the evidence adduced by the respondents did not prove the existence of any temple in favour of which the original grant was alleged to have been made according to them. It further held that the finding of the trial court that the appellants were the owners of the properties in dispute was correct. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The decision of the High Court was based upon no evidence at all. [847 C] (ii) The High Court was right in holding that the evidence produced by the respondents showed that the original grants had been transferred by the manager to the appellants. [848 D] (iii) The High Courts had taken the view that the burden of proving that the originals of the grant had been transferred was on the respondents. The burden was on the party alleging the transfer to prove it. [849 E] Gnanasambanda vs Gnanasama, I.L.R. , referred to.
4641: The appellants, who were partners of a firm, applied to the District Magistrate for permission to construct a modern Cinema Hall at the Apsara Theatre situated at Gandhi Nagar, Jammu. The application was rejected by the District Magistrate on the ground that the licence had been granted in the name of one Shri Ved Gupta and not in the name and style of the firm. The appellants filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of the District Magistrate. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the renewal of the licence could not be made in the name 'of any party other than the original licensee, namely, Shri Ved Gupta, who had been declared to be the sole licensee in respect of the Apsar Cinema. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the renewal could not be refused because the licence had become impossible for him to operate the cinema in question. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The grant of the licence in favour of Shri Ved Gupta is not an act of privilege or a privilege within the meaning of section 3(1) of the . It is only a licence which is issued under the Act and the Rules framed thereunder. [839E] 2. The grant or renewal of a licence is not a matter of right but is subject to certain conditions. The grantor has a right to refuse the grant if he thinks fit. The grantee has no right to insist upon the grantor to have his licence renewed. [840F] 3. The grantees are entitled to use the premises for the purpose of their business. They cannot be heard to say that they will not be able to do so. The grantors are entitled to take the benefit of the provisions of the Act and Rules. [841G] 4. The grant is not a mere licence. It is merely a licence. It does not create any interest in the property. It is only the licensee who is held responsible for the acts done by the licensee. He can be said to be in possession of the premises. [842C] 5. The grant must be for the purpose specified in the Act and rules. [843D] 6. The grant may be for a particular purpose
380: The appellants were displaced persons, and on 30 8 1952 the respondent issued a notice to them under section 7 of the . On 31 8 1952 the appellants entered into an agreement with them, Exhibit C, which contained a clause that the appellants would be put in possession of the mills and the factory on 31 8 1952. On 30 8 1952, the respondent issued another notice to the appellants, stating that the appellants had committed breaches of the various terms on which the properties had been leased to them, and calling upon them to show cause why the lease should not be cancelled and they should be evicted. The appellants replied to the notice but did not pay any heed to it. The Custodian General, however, passed an order cancelling the lease. The appellants filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the order. The High Court held that the Custodian had power under section 12 of the , to cancel the lease and that the appellants could not be said to have contravened the provisions of section 10 of the Act. Held, that the Custodian was competent to issue the notice under section 7 and the High Court erred in holding that the appellants were guilty of breach of the provisions of sections 10 and 12 of the Act, and that the order of cancellation of the lease was bad. The powers conferred by section 12 are wide enough to include the power to cancel the leases granted by the evacuee and not to terminate the lease.

652: The appellants were carrying on business in cotton and groundnut. They filed writ petitions in the High Court of Madras challenging the validity of the provisions of the Madras Commercial Crops Markets Act, 1933, as amended by the Madras Agricultural Produce Marketing (Regulation) Amendment Act, 1954, and the Rules framed thereunder. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the provisions of section 5(4)(a) of the Act were void to the extent it conferred on the Collector authority to refuse a licence at his own discretion and rule 37 was void in so far as it prohibited persons whose names had not yet been registered as buyers and sellers, from carrying on business. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The provisions of the Act and the Rules made thereunder constitute an unreasonable restriction upon the appellants ' fundamental right to carry on business under article 19(1)(g). The Act is a law relating to trade and commerce within the meaning of entry 48 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. It is well settled that the State Legislature has exclusive power to legislate with respect to any of the matters enumerated in List I and List III of the Seventh schedule to the Constitution subject to the limitations imposed by Parliament by virtue of entries 77 and 78 of List I. The legislative competence of the State Legislature is limited by the restrictions which may be placed by Parliament by way of legislation with respect to one or more of the matters in List I. [550 C D] The impugned Act does not impose any restrictions on the petitioners ' fundamental rights under article 19 (1) (g) of the Constitution. The impugned Act imposes restrictions on the right to acquire, hold and dispose of property and the said restrictions are reasonable restrictions within the meaning Of article 19(6) of the constitution. [552 E F; 553 A B] The impugned provisions do not offend against the guarantee of freedom of trade guaranteed by article 301 of the Constitution and are therefore invalid. [553 G H]

4807: The appellant was appointed as a Head Clerk on an ad hoc basis in January 1974. He was promoted as a Head clerk on April 1, 1975 and he continued to work as such till March 14, 1976. On April 1, 1976 the appellant was appointed a regular employee of the Panchayat Samiti as a head clerk. On April 2, 1976 the Government notified the absorption of the appellant as a clerk, though, as stated earlier, he was working as a head Clerk in the Loharu Panchayat Samiti. On April 3, 1976 the State Government notified the absorbtion of the appellant in the Panchayat Samiti. The appellant challenged his appointment by way of writ petition before the High Court which dismissed it holding that the appellant was entitled to be absorbed in the Panchayat. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the appellant had been appointed as a head clerks prior to his absorption in the Panchayat and therefore he could not be considered for promotion to the post of a Head Clerk. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The appellant was entitled under section 14(4) of the Amending Act, 1973 to continue in the service of the Panchayat on the same terms and conditions on which he was employed by the Panchayat Samiti until he was absorbed in the Government service. [739E] (2) The fact that the appellant is promoted as a head constable on an adhoc basis in January, 1974 or the further fact that he was appointed as such on April 1. 1975, cannot improve his position for the simple reason that these appointments were made after June 13, 1973 when the Amending Act came into force. [740F G] (3) The question whether the appellant was rightly absorbed in the service or not has to be decided in the light of the provisions of section 14(6) of the Amendment Act. [741A]

4917: The petitioners in the writ petitions were working as Lecturers in Government Higher Secondary Schools and other institutions. They had been serving in the State of Andhra Pradesh for more than 30 years. Their case is that they were entitled to be considered for promotion to the post of Headmaster/Headmistress in the schools run by the State Government. The Government of Andhra Pradesh issued a notification dated October 29, 1979 fixing the age of retirement from 58 to 55. By another notification dated October 9, 1980, the Government of Andhra pradesh also increased the age of superannuation from 55 to 58 years. In the meanwhile, the Government had taken a decision to reduce the age of superannuating teachers from 55 to 55. The Government had not given any notice to the employees who had retired prior to the date on which the age of their superannuation was increased to 55. On the other hand, the Government took a policy decision to reduce their age of retirement to 55. This decision was taken after considering the representations made by the employees. The Government has acted unreasonably in reducing the age of the employees to 55. It is stated that the Government had acted unreasonably without having regard to the factors relevant on the fixation of the age of retir ement. The petitioners contended that there was no basis at all for reduction of the age. The respondents in the writ petition contended that the Government was estopped from reducing the age. Dismissing the writ petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The Government was bound to give an opportunity to the employees to make representation against the proposed reduction of the retirement age. [550F] 2. The Government cannot take advantage of its own wrong. [551G H] 3. The Government is bound to act reasonably within the four corners of law. [552A] 4. The Government can fix the age of a government employee at 55 or 58. But the Government cannot take away the right of the employees. [553C] 5. The Government should have given due consideration to the representations made against the proposed change in the age of 60. [554E]
6622: The appellant was a dealer in milk and milk products. He purchased certain goods from the respondent for his personal use and sold them to others. The sales tax authorities held that the appellant was liable to pay purchase tax on the purchase value of the goods at the time when they were purchased, but that he was not liable to pay tax on the price actually paid by him. The High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the words "disposes of" used in clause (a)(ii) of sub section (1) of section 5 of the Act did not include cases of despatches by a dealer of the manufactured goods otherwise than by way of sale as, for example, by way of stock transfer. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression "disposal of goods" used in cl.(b) of sub s.(1) of s.5 of the is not confined to cases of dispatches only. It does not extend to cases of disposal of goods by way of Stock Transfer. [353D] 2. The word "disposal" has been used in the proviso to sub section (2) of section 3 of the Act. The word 'disposal ' is defined in section 2(c) of the Act to mean "the disposal of goods or any part thereof by means of sale or other arrangement or by any other mode otherwise than by sale in the course of inter State trade or commerce". The word "sale" is defined in the Explanation to the said section to mean "a transfer of property in goods involved in the execution of works contract which takes place outside the State or in the course o f inter state trade or commerce or in the execution or works p erty of any other similar work." [354E F; 355A B]
1329: The appellants were registered dealers under the Bombay Sales Tax Act, 1950. The Sales Tax Officer rejected this claim for exemption and assessed them to purchase tax under section 10(b) of the Bombay Sales 'Tax Act, 1950, as a "registered dealer ". The appellants moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the order of assessment and the notice of demand and for restraining the Sales Tax Officer from taking any steps pursuant to the order or the notice. The High Court held that the sale of the goods was not in the course of export but only in the course when the goods passed to the buyers at the time of their sale and that the sale must be deemed to have taken place in the course.of export. Held: (i) that the sale in question did not fall within the expression "in the course of" in article 286(1)(b) of Constitution and therefore the sales were not taxable. (ii)that the sale in the present case was not in course of export and the sales were in the course, of export. (iii)that the sales were effected by the appellants in the course and import of the goods and not in the export of the goods. (iv)that the appellants were entitled to the benefit of article 286(2) of the Constitution. (v)that the High Court erred in holding that the appellants were liable to pay tax under section 9(1)(a) of the Act.
3893: The appellant divorced the respondent in 1965. She filed a suit for maintenance against her husband and his family members. The trial court held that she was a divorcee and awarded monthly allowance of Rs. 300/ for the son and Rs. 400/ for the mother for their subsistence, taking due note of the fact that the cost of living in Bombay, where the parties lived, was high and that the respondent had provided residential accommodation to the appellant. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the courts below were wrong in holding that the appellant was a divorce and awarding monthly allowance of a sum of Rs. 200/ for the maintenance of herself and her child; (ii) the Explanation to section 125(1)(b) of the Code is not applicable to a case of a divorce between the husband and wife; (iii) the Explanation does not apply to a case where the husband has contracted a second marriage during the life time of the first wife or has contracted a third marriage during the lifetime of the first husband; (iv) the Explanation applies only when there is a decree of divorce passed by a competent court; (v) the Explanation is not applicable as the Explanation applies to cases where the husband is a Hindu and the wife is a Hindu. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Explanation to section 127(3)(b) applies only when the husband has a decree of nullity under section 12(2) of the Act. [801 G] 2. The Explanation applies only where the husband and the wife are Hindus. [802 A B] 3. The Explanation does not come into play in a case where there is a divorce decree. It is only where the wife is treated as a Muslim by the husband that the Explanation would apply. [803 C D] 4. The Explanation is not intended to be used to cut down the scope of the definition of "wife" contained in section 125 of the Criminal Procedure Code. The Explanation cannot be interpreted so as to include a woman who has been divorced by the husband before the commencement of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1976. [804 E F]

6413: The appellant was convicted under section 5(2) read with section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947.
